newsitem.title: USA: US TREASURIES NEAR SESSION LOWS IN EARLY AFTERNOON.
newsitem.headline: US TREASURIES NEAR SESSION LOWS IN EARLY AFTERNOON.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices were trading near session lows on Monday after early gains failed to attract followthrough buying.

Bargain-hunting had given prices a lift at the start of the trading session. But analysts predicted gains would be capped by concerns that the U.S. July retail sales report, due on Wednesday, might show that consumer spending picked up in the first month of the third quarter after easing in the second quarter.
At 1200 EDT/1600 GMT, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was down 8/32 to 96-12/32, yielding 6.66 percent. In contrast, the 30-year bond was up 8/32 at the start of the session.
The yield curve steepened during the session, extending a trend that began on Thursday, shortly after the Treasury announced the results of its $10.0 billion 30-year bond sale.

With two-year notes still up 2/32 to 99-26/32 at midday, exactly where they were priced near the start of the session, the spread between two- and 30-year yields had steepened to 68 basis points from 64 basis points earlier and 57 basis points at the close on Wednesday.

"After the significant market setback on Friday, it made sense that there was an attempt to generate some buying interest (overseas)," said Alan Levenson, director of research at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co Inc. "But in the U.S., there's so much trepidation about the data coming out -- particularly about retail sales -- that it was hard to hold the gains."
Economists polled by Reuters offered an average forecast of a 0.7 percent gain in July retail sales.
And Levenson said, "Curve steepening will be the rule if we're entering an extended bear phase -- I believe we are."
On that assumption, Levenson said, it was necessary for participants "to respect the levels of interst rates that we can attain when we do move into a bear market.

"Just because we've gone to roughly six percent on the two-year (note yield) doesn't mean we should buy them," he said. "Because we could get up to 6.40 percent of 6.50 percent on the two-years and 7.10 percent of 7.20 percent on bonds."
Levenson said there was no reason to conclude Friday's setback was just a correction and that the market would soon return to its lows on rates.
The 6-3/8 percent 30-year bond stood at 96-17/32 at midday, yielding 6.64 percent, compared with 98-18/32 at Monday's New York close.

The trader at the brokerage house said: "While (prices of) Treasuries have been falling since Friday's drop, some traders missed out on a chance to sell... If Treasuries decline again, selling pressure from those traders will accelerate the speed of a fall."
Meanwhile, a trader at a Japanese bank said that strong retail sales data could spur further selling, but a drop in Treasury prices will be limited due to buying interest on dips.
Retail sales for July are expected to show a rise of 0.7 percent, or 0.5 percent if cars are excluded, on Wednesday.

The trader at the Japanese bank added that he would also focus on moves in the dollar. "It depends on how you look at the recent weakness in the dollar. If the dollar falls again versus the mark or the yen, then Treasuries will be sold too," he said. The U.S. currency stood near 1.8628/38 marks and 115.90/00 yen at 0337 GMT.
The September T-bond futures contract stood at 112-25/32 at 0337 GMT, little changed from 112-24/32 at the previous close.
